title: Super funds sharpen appetite for infrastructure assets
full_text:
Australian institutional investors are increasingly turning to infrastructure and unlisted property as they seek to balance long-term returns with protection against inflation and economic volatility, new research has found.
IFM Investors’ 2026 Private Markets 700 report found 75 per cent of Australian investors and advisers planned to increase their infrastructure equity allocations over the next three to five years, compared with 63 per cent globally.
The findings were drawn from a survey of 700 senior investment professionals conducted by FT Longitude for IFM Investors during May and June. Participants included 267 professionals from pension and superannuation funds, alongside representatives from insurers, wealth managers and investment consultancies.
Another 60 per cent of Australian respondents planned to lift their exposure to unlisted real estate, exceeding the global result of 48 per cent.
The report said Australia’s longstanding superannuation industry, which has invested in infrastructure and property for decades, may partly explain the country’s stronger appetite for real assets.
Pension and super funds globally also showed a preference for infrastructure debt, with 63 per cent planning to increase their allocations over the next three to five years, compared with 55 per cent of all respondents.
Australian respondents appeared more comfortable investing internationally, with 59 per cent holding investments through globally diversified vehicles, compared with 37 per cent globally.
However, their allocation plans varied considerably across private market asset classes. The report found that one third of Australian investors expected to reduce their private debt exposure over the next three to five years, compared with 21 per cent of respondents worldwide.
Liquidity also remained a prominent consideration, with 68 per cent of Australian respondents saying greater liquidity and more flexible redemption terms would encourage further private market investment, compared with 39 per cent globally.
Broader concerns about inflation and economic instability were shaping those allocation decisions, with only 21 per cent of respondents believing their portfolios could consistently perform across a wide range of economic conditions.
Infrastructure equity emerged as the most popular private market asset class globally, narrowly ahead of private equity. Some 63 per cent planned to increase infrastructure equity allocations, while 62 per cent intended to add to private equity.
IFM Investors head of infrastructure for Europe, Deepa Bharadwaj, said the characteristics of infrastructure could help explain its appeal to institutional investors.
“Infrastructure assets provide essential services that need to be available 24/7, and typically have strong demand through cycles,” Bharadwaj said. “Combined with limited competition, these characteristics are a foundation for inflation hedging and resilience.”
Competition for assets associated with artificial intelligence and other long-term themes was nevertheless creating valuation concerns, with 62 per cent of respondents saying capital inflows into these areas were putting pressure on future returns.
UniSuper head of private markets, Sandra Lee, said investors could look beyond heavily contested assets for exposure to these structural trends.
“Data centres have become a crowded space, but investors can invest in the smaller businesses that service data centres and essential infrastructure, where competition may be lower,” Lee said. “For example, we’ve invested in a business supporting grid infrastructure, which gives us direct exposure to the growing power demands of data centres and data usage.”
Lee said deeper relationships with a smaller group of investment managers could also give asset owners better access and control.
“Our ‘smart partnerships’ approach means working with a small number of highly rated managers and going deeper in those relationships. That can give us priority access to high-quality deal flow, co-investment opportunities and governance rights, while giving us the support of partners with local expert teams on the ground.”
